This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee, and this was an evidence session to scrutinize the Welsh Government's progress in developing the new curriculum for Wales. The particular focus of this year's conference was on the issue of assessment and they were joined by colleagues from Scotland, from Ireland, from Iceland, from Finland, from Saskatchewan, from Nova Scotia and from Uruguay. Kirsty Williams AM started by introducing the main messages that had been received during the feedback period on the draft curriculum. There was broad support for the curriculum changes that they were proposing. Also, there was a concerted effort and a plan drawn up to try and ensure that there was as much engagement, knowledge and opportunity as possible. They also held a number of focus group sessions specifically for young people themselves, so that they could give them their feedback. There were 24 focus groups that were arranged for children and young people. Assessment had been a crucial part of the process that they had been involved in. They had embraced experts who were involved in that process who were part of their curriculum assessment group.

Kirsty Williams AM first introduced that the original proposal that they began working on was to provide for the four purposes—so, in the legislation, to provide  four purposes. Then, below that, they were going to legislate for a number of the cross-curricular aspects. They would make a statutory provision for the 'what matters' statements. In terms of progression steps, there would be a statutory framework to ensure that there was breadth within the curriculum for everybody, and they would bring it a step lower again to bring it down again to what matters statements within that, again providing greater certainty and greater clarity about the expectations at a national level. With regard to RSE, the key messages were focused on whether children should be taught RSE at all and that this should not be in the curriculum and it shouldn't be a compulsory part of the curriculum—that this was not an area where the school system and the education system should be involved, and it should be left to the preserve of parents to teach children about issues around relationships and sexuality education.

Kirsty Williams AM explained that the original proposal that they began working on was to provide for the four purposes, which included putting in law the areas of learning and experience. Then, below that, they were going to legislate for a number of the cross-curricular aspects, including literacy, the numeracy and the digital competency. The two main new areas that they were now working on to include within the Bill were to ensure that there is breadth within the curriculum for everybody, and they would make a statutory provision for the 'what matters' statements. They would also be looking to include in the legislation provision for a statutory framework setting out their approach to progression in each of the AoLE areas.

The 'what matters' statements would include broad concepts of what matters, what we believe matters, in the areas of learning and experience, and they would now actually put into the legislation. They would also be looking to include in the legislation provision for a statutory framework setting out their approach to progression in each of the AoLE areas. They were proposing those changes because of responses that they had had. One of the consistent worries that some people had had, whilst being very supportive of the overall aims, was how to get that balance between individual autonomy in the school, but also ensure that there was some national expectation and that the variation on these important things was not so great as to cause concern. Kirsty Williams AM answered that they would demonstrate that they were listening to people, that there had been concern expressed about certainty and having a national approach on some of these issues and they had taken steps to address that and still left huge flexibility underneath as to how to approach those, which particular topics to select in how to actually teach them.

According to Kirsty Williams, the government valued the work done by the Wales Institute of Social and Economic Research, Data and Methods and the presentation so far and the paper to be presented by Dr Nigel Newton. The institutions were able to work in networks to provide support to a network of schools, which was not available in the Scottish system. It was not a criticism of them; it was just that they had got a structure that they could utilise to do that support so that schools were not completely left on their own and they could be working with other schools, with their regional consortia, going forward. At a regional level, they require the regions to engage with all schools through the cluster model.

The WISERD research suggested that there should be a clear distinction between assessment for learning and an accountability in the system, otherwise they drive—inadvertently; people don't set out to do it, but they drive a set of behaviours that have negative unintended outcomes. When it comes to the assessment of pupils for their own progression and the evaluation of how a school does at certain points in its life cycle, there is a thick black line between these two concepts.

The first thing to realise was that their curriculum was not a copycat of the Scottish curriculum, but it was always useful to reflect on how other systems had undertaken curriculum reform in their nation and to learn from any issues that had arisen. Kirsty Williams AM also pointed out that the strong middle tier and the role that the middle tier was playing in Wales, which was absent in Scotland, made a difference, and they were interested in looking at some of the practices that other countries used to include pupil voice to find out what's happening.

All of the schools that had previously been pioneers were invited to apply to morph into the next phase, which is innovation schools. The innovation schools had led to a specific piece of work as they did the final refinement, and their main role was working with us on these final refinements to the content but also to the assessment issues and accountability issues.

Children's rights, human rights—they had been key considerations throughout the design, and this was currently set out in overarching guidance and they continued to work with the children's commissioner's office to map the rights of the child across each area of learning and experience. And Kirsty Williams AM was delighted that the Children's commissioner took the time to write to me during the feedback phase to say that they were very pleased that their initial assessment demonstrates that what we're proposing is a big step forward.

According to Kirsty, they have a separate programme of work that is looking at resources that are needed to support the curriculum. They have already had conversations with Qualifications Wales yesterday to try to avoid the debacle that they had previously, where they had new qualifications and the resources to support those qualifications weren't available. And this proposal by the Learned Society will be considered as part of that work.

According to Kirsty Williams, there would be progression points on that continuum that would show progression both in Welsh language and in the English language, and they had to be contextualised. They recognize that children learning Welsh in a Welsh-medium school, their progressional on that point would be more speedy and quicker, and by the end of primary school they would be in a very different position than a child that was learning English in an English-language school. So, they have to contextualise that learning continuum depending on the medium of tuition with the school, but recognising that it is a progression. It isn't a start and never get any further.

This was the first meeting of the new remote control project. The project manager announced that they would make a profit of fifty million Euros by selling twenty-five million units in Europe. To make the profit, they would have to use a big market in Europe and sell fifty million units. The remote control would be made in three parts. The basic things would be on the same place, like on off button on top and the TV channels one two three four as a block, and then the volume obviously on top, so that users could see. But the rest was not used that often, so if they had a clear button with an good icon on it, it should be clear as well. They could do something unique with that.

The group discussed the functional design of the remote control, including the components, properties and the specifications of the user interface. They also talked about some possible advanced techniques, such as the folding of the control, the positioning of the buttons and the small touch screen. Then they discussed some possible functions, including setting the volume, controlling TV channels and controlling other devices.

The Project Manager thought that the remote control was just a black thing with some buttons on it, which was not very special, but the team could try to make it special. The Project Manager believed that a good remote control should be able to be used from everywhere in the room, so that kids and the elderly could use it, and the infrared should be of good quality.

The Marketing thought that a remote control that could fold open and look like a mobile phone would be too expensive. He believed that remote controls were most things in the house that fell down on the ground and got often broken, so the remote control would not be as strong as a normal one. Besides, he believed that children would not play with it because it was too fragile.

Industrial Designer suggested to think of a small touch screen on the remote control, which could be installed to make it easy to use and small, so that the buttons that users used often could be put in usable places, and the on/off button could be placed on top so that users could see. In addition, Industrial Design suggested that the basic things should be put on the same place, like on off button on top and the TV channels one two three four as a block, and then the volume obviously on top, so users can see. The remote control could be made to be user-friendly by having a clear button with an icon on it so that it would be clear when users did not use that often.

The remote control should be designed with the basic functions in mind, such as turning on the TV, adjusting channels, adjusting the volume, and so on. The shape and appearance of the remote control shall be determined by the market and user requirements.

The User Interface suggested to put the basic things on the same place, like on off button on top and the TV channels one two three four as a block, and then the volume obviously on top, so that users could see. He believed that it didn't matter what place it was on the remote control, it should be clear and unique.

Marketing mentioned that younger people under the age of forty five were more interested in new features, while older people were more content with keeping the old things. Therefore, Marketing suggested that the team could skip speech recognition altogether.

User Interface disagreed with Marketing's suggestion on the ease of use because there were already many controls out that supported a lot of stuff. This was the third meeting of the remote control project. The team failed to reach the target group because they got the information at the wrong time. Also, the price was not included on the budget list so they couldn't make a fancy prototype out of it. Therefore, they had to settle with a one for fancy look-and-feel and a seven for new features.

Marketing made evaluation criteria from one to zero. The criteria included creativity, innovativeness, style, new features, target audience, color, material, logo, battery, power indicator, battery recharger, etc. The average score for each criterion was given as one.

The team agreed that the scrollwheel was easy to use, but the second layer was not so easy. The team also agreed that speech, the scroll wheel and the slide were new and innovative. Therefore, they gave it a two out of seven.

Marketing recommended to give an average score from one to zero on the criteria of market trend. The average score should indicate whether the product reached the target group beneath forty. If it did not, then the product was not extraordinary new or something and the average score would be one.

The group discussed the cost of the battery, the advanced chip and the sample speaker. Then they discussed the size of the front and the shape of the back. Finally, they agreed to use the drawing board as a favourite for their text.

User Interface thought they got the wrong information at the wrong time when discussing the project finance. The prices could be twenty Euros or something now, and if they had fifteen Euros, then they would gap it. This was the biggest problem.

This was the second meeting of the new remote control project. The first was about the price, which was 12.5 Euros. The second was about leadership and teamwork, and the third was about product evaluation.

Marketing presented the evaluation criteria based on the user requirements and trends found in the marketing reports and marketing strategy of the company. The criteria included fancy look and feel, technological innovation, easy to use, incorporation of current fashion trends, minimization of RSI, easy locating, innovation for money's sake, beeper function, etc. Then the group rated each criterion individually on a seven-point scale.

Marketing thought that the incorporation of current fashion trends in the prototype was a good idea, especially in relation to the market research findings about the spongy texture to the exterior and the fruit and vegetable design colors. However, he did not agree with the group mates on whether to use voice recognition because it might be biased.

The remote control had the highest rating of meeting the specifications that was definitely true for two of the six criteria. It incorporated current fashion trends and was easy to locate. The lowest rating was close to neutral on the minimization of repetitive strain injury. It was high enough at the upper end of the scale for the team to go ahead with the product, but on the basis of current technology and capabilities, they could actually do much more to minimize that on such a small device.

The team was satisfied with the cost of the remote control. However, they still had some budget issues to deal with, like overheads and heating for the building. After that, they agreed to take voice recognition out of the price and set the price at 12.5 Euros.

User Interface thought that the replacement of the kinetic batteries would not make a big difference because customers never said anything about the battery and nobody looked into the battery. The shape and colours of the remote control were not important to customers, so it should not be compared with other kinds of batteries.

Industrial Designer asked whether the incorporation of voice recognition would make the cost of the remote control lower or higher. Marketing suggested that it would be feasible to incorporate the voice recognition initially to business class customers because customers were willing to pay more for better products and it also set the product apart from the crowd. Project Manager agreed and added that they could choose to have the feature for business class or something else if they wanted it.

This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee's sixth evidence session for their inquiry on education otherwise than at school. It was mainly about the increase in the number of children and young people being excluded from school in Wales. The main reasons were more examples of very challenging behaviour, the prevalence of ASD spectrum disorder, and trying to get the learners the right provision was sometimes a challenge. Also, the report highlighted the importance of the school being inclusive, and for that child, regardless of whether they had an additional learning need or not, to have proper opportunity to progress. Next, the committee discussed the transition arrangements for pupils who were in a PRU and then trying to return to the main school setting.

Sian Gwenllian AM asked about the funding of the additional learning needs sector which was adversely affected by the new Act coming into force. In response to this question, David Hopkins said that the delegation levels were already very high in most authority areas, and they had got agreements in place with the Government to make sure that more money, or as much money as possible, was devolved to schools. However, in fairness to PRUs, they had been trying to work on the fact that, if children moved out of school, the funding followed them, so they should not want a lag in the system, because they had to meet the challenge of the pupils, but the money was still in the schools, because it was once a year that they had that funding. In terms of the Samaritans report, it was suggested that funding tended to go into diagnosis rather than support, so the group discussed how to balance this issue. In the end, they agreed to work out what was the best support at this point in time for the young person.

The new Act aimed at tackling the problem of truancy, and David Hopkins believed that it would put pressure on local authorities and schools, especially the post-16 sector, as they were talking now about a wider age range—doing up to 25 as well. However, David Hopkins also admitted that there were financial pressures there, but he did not think the levels of delegation had any impact on that. He believed that the delegation levels were already very high in most authority areas, and they had agreements in place with the Government to make sure that more money or as much money as possible, was devolved to schools.

The narrow measure at the end of key stage 4 attainment, which he thought had put pressure on some schools, certainly, and headteachers had felt that—sometimes excluded, or otherwise put into another school as a consequence, which was regrettable, but that's what's happened. And on the additional learning needs side, whilst the Minister had currently made some more money available, he knew from the experiences that ALN funding had become increasingly under pressure, and local authorities at one point almost gave up going to tribunals, because they were losing them time and time again. David Hopkins did not think that the delegation levels were a direct factor because they had agreements in place with the Government to make sure that more money or as much money as possible, was devolved to schools.

There was a better sharing of practice between the PRU sector and the local authorities. Also, the team had recognized that sometimes a child would find themselves at home because they were not able to get back into the school setting, the main school setting. They had built a brand-new PRU provision in Swansea, which would be open in January 2021, and they had their staff working very closely with the schools.

According to Sharon Davies, it was very difficult to plan ahead, and from year to year and also within the term, because it changes so much, it's difficult to adapt to the changing situation. Moreover, the provision for more learners coming in or moving, and then that causes the pressure within the system, because they haven't planned for them, and therefore there's no spare funding there to draw on. Also, in fairness to PRUs, they've been trying to work on the fact that, if children move out of school, the funding follows them, so they want them reintegrated back into schools.

The answer was that it was a question of the whole school environment and how that interacts with the challenges that a young person might be facing. One was that they wanted to promote a compassionate response and an informed response by everybody in the school to distressed young people, and that distress may show in a number of ways, not necessarily just as obvious distress. Another was to connect this with the agenda around adverse childhood experiences, and to make sure that teachers were aware of the link between inequality and all the things that come under that term, and challenging behaviour, so that more teachers would be equipped with the skills to deal with those really challenging situations.

Janet Finch-Saunders asked about the advantages and disadvantages of local authoritative frameworks. Nick Williams answered that they did that, but they were struggling sometimes for additional provision. First and foremost, safeguarding was at the forefront of their thinking. However, they needed to perhaps think about how the staff in that sort of additional provision would have. At the moment, they were managing those pressures in their own provision whilst they went out and observed through a provision framework to make sure that the provision was.

As a local authority, they were restricted on how much access they could get into the home, which meant that unless the families invited them in, there was very little to quality assure. Local authorities should also take charge of the quality assurance of alternative provision, which they had set out their own TCP—Torfaen curriculum panel which looked at alternative provision. The meetings were facilitated and they were currently undergoing a review of the alternate provisions each school was doing because, sometimes, it had worked in the past, but what they were seeing now was that it was not quite working now, and it was understanding why.

According to David Hopkins, they were not in a position to answer fully as to what was going on because there was not really a national picture that they could pick up in terms of data or information regarding this, but what they did know was that there was a push towards seeing this in the curriculum. Then they discussed some other forms of provision, like home tuition, which they were also restricted on how much access they got into the home. Finally, they agreed that it was important to see this as a preventative agenda.

The committee members expressed concern about the shortage of qualified teachers and educational psychologists in the special education provision. They agreed that it was a capacity issue, because if they took them out of the provision, it would be difficult for a supply teacher to come in and manage that class because of the demands, so they needed a group of people in the future to fill those gaps. They talked a lot about certificates and so forth, and qualifications, but ensuring everybody's well-being was important, and an important outcome of the work. Then they discussed the problem of the staff leaving and there were very small numbers of staff working in that provision. There really isn't the capacity for them to access professional training.

According to Nick Williams, it came down to additional funding, because he would like a dedicated educational psychologist spending their time possibly only with PRU youngsters and EOTAS provision, but they haven't got the capacity because of the demands on them from the wider system. Also, it was also about ensuring the right staff as well, because sometimes, they may have them, but if they move on or retire, or whatever, there's not a bus load of people with the expertise. It was really difficult to start all over again.

According to Nick Williams, there had been provision in the north and south of the county, but even so, the distances that those learners were having to travel were huge. In conclusion, some of the areas had been covered, while others still needed further investigation.

The third requirement was that the product should focus on customers that were younger than forty because the corporate image should be recognisable in the product.

Industrial Designer thought that the remote control should use infrared because otherwise it would be hard for it to communicate with almost every TV set. User Interface proposed to install a base station next to the TV set to prevent customers from losing their remote controls. Project Manager agreed but pointed out that this would be costly. Then the team discussed clapping technique and decided to use a round button instead of a stick.

Industrial Designer pointed out that the remote control should use energy-sparse, friendly components which consume far less power than conventional components. For cost-effectiveness, they should really use a very low-cost circuit board because most of the production cost were in this part of the equipment. User Interface suggested that they could use rechargeable LEDs but they were a little bit more expensive. Industrial Designer agreed and added that a cradle was also feasible.

This was the second meeting of the detailed design of the remote control. Last time, they had discussed the squishy fruitiness of their remote controls and how they might pursue that.
